Puritan Doctrine
PYOOR-ih-tan DOK-trin
n. phrase (historical theology; English Reformation; practical piety)
From Latin purus (pure, unmixed) through English Puritan (one who desires to purify the Church of England further from Roman Catholic forms and doctrine); doctrina (teaching, instruction); the term “Puritan doctrine” designates the theological convictions and practical applications that characterized the English and American Puritan movement (c. 1560–1700) — not a single uniform system but a family of Reformed convictions applied with thoroughness to every sphere of life. The Puritans were Calvinists in soteriology, Congregationalists or Presbyterians in ecclesiology, and experimentalists in spirituality.

Biblical Definition

Puritan doctrine is distinguished not by novel theological content but by the thoroughness with which the Puritans applied Reformed soteriology to the conscience, the heart, and the whole of common life. The Puritans were heirs of the Reformation but critics of its English application: they believed the Church of England had reformed its doctrine while leaving its worship cluttered with Roman ceremonies and its discipline slack. Their governing question was Psalm 119:9 — “How can a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed according to Your word.” Scripture, not tradition or royal decree, was the standard for every area of life. They applied the Word with the same intensity to private prayer, family worship, business ethics, magistracy, and warfare that their Continental predecessors had applied to dogmatic controversy. Christ's prayer in John 17:17 was their sanctification charter: “Sanctify them in the truth; Your word is truth.” The means of sanctification was immersion in the revealed Word, not mystical infusion or sacramental channel. Paul's charge to Timothy in 2 Timothy 2:15 captures the Puritan epistemological posture: “Be diligent to present yourself approved to God — a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.” The Puritan preacher was above all a worker in the Word, expending effort in preparation and in application so that the congregation's consciences were reached. Colossians 3:16 supplied the model for corporate worship: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly — teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.” The Puritans' regulative-principle application of this text produced a worship stripped of vestments, ceremonies, and set prayers, centered on preaching and psalmody.

Webster 1828 Definition

Puritan doctrine is the theological and practical application of Reformed soteriology to every sphere of life — governed by Scripture alone, centered on experimental knowledge of grace, distinguished by thorough-going application of the Word to conscience, family, church, and commonwealth, and systematized in the Westminster Standards as the Puritans' enduring confessional legacy.

PURITAN DOCTRINE, n. phrase (historical theology; English Reformation). The theological convictions and practical applications of the English and American Puritan movement (c. 1560–1700): Reformed in soteriology, biblicist in worship, experimental in spirituality, and comprehensive in the application of divine revelation to every sphere of creaturely life.

The core of Puritan soteriology is Calvinist in the fullest sense: total depravity, unconditional election, definite atonement, irresistible grace, and perseverance of the saints — the five heads articulated against the Remonstrants at the Synod of Dort (1618–1619). But the Puritans pressed these doctrines into the heart's experience in a way that Continental Reformed theology had not always done. William Perkins (d. 1602), the first major Puritan systematician, developed the “practical syllogism” as the method by which the elect could examine their hearts for genuine conversion: the general promise of the gospel (major premise) + the evidence of faith and repentance in one's own experience (minor premise) = assurance of election (conclusion). This experimental approach to assurance became the Puritan distinctive that set them apart from both the antinomian (who claimed assurance without examination) and the legalist (who grounded assurance in performance).

Puritan worship theology is governed by the regulative principle of worship: only what God has commanded in Scripture is permitted in corporate worship; what He has not commanded is prohibited. This produced a stark contrast with the Church of England's retention of vestments, liturgical ceremony, and episcopacy, which the Puritans viewed as unwarranted additions to divine prescription. The Directory for Public Worship (1645), produced by the Westminster Assembly, is the Puritan worship standard: its approach replaced the Book of Common Prayer's fixed liturgy with free prayer guided by principle, and its preaching theology shaped a generation of expository preachers.

The family was the Puritan's primary institution for spiritual formation. The father as the household priest, daily family worship, catechizing of children and servants, and the Puritan Sabbath — strictly observed from Saturday sunset to Sunday sunset — were the practical architecture of Puritan godliness. This domestic theology was not merely tradition but exegesis: the household codes of Ephesians 5–6 and Colossians 3–4 applied with the same rigor the Puritans applied to church order.

The Westminster Standards (Westminster Confession of Faith, Larger Catechism, Shorter Catechism) are the Puritans' doctrinal monument. The Shorter Catechism's first answer — “Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy Him forever” — encapsulates the Puritan vision: the whole of life redirected toward the one sufficient end, from which all other ends derive their legitimacy. The American Puritan inheritors, particularly the New England Congregationalists and the Presbyterians of the Middle Colonies, carried this vision into the founding generation of the American republic.

Key Scripture

Psalm 119:9 — "How can a young man cleanse his way? By taking heed according to Your word."

John 17:17 — "Sanctify them in the truth. Your word is truth."

2 Timothy 2:15 — "Be diligent to present yourself approved to God — a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth."

Colossians 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, in all wisdom — teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs — singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God."

Modern Corruption

Romantic historiography caricatures the Puritans as joyless, repressive, and theocratic; revisionist historians credit them with producing the “Protestant work ethic” at the expense of their piety; liberal Protestantism harvests Puritan social vision while discarding their dogmatic core — all three distortions evacuate the doctrinal substance that produced the culture the critics alternately decry and appropriate.

expand to see more

The caricature of the Puritans as grim, pleasure-hating theocrats has its origins in Enlightenment anti-clericalism and was popularized by H.L. Mencken's quip that Puritanism is “the haunting fear that someone, somewhere, may be happy.” The historical record refutes this portrait at every point. Richard Sibbes (d. 1635) wrote with pastoral tenderness that has rarely been surpassed; John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress is suffused with joy; Samuel Rutherford's letters burn with affectionate longing for Christ; Thomas Watson called the Lord's Day the queen of days and the day of believers' greatest delight. The Puritans were not anti-pleasure; they were anti-false-pleasure — they pursued the highest pleasures (communion with God, study of Scripture, family worship, honest labor, godly friendship) with intensity, precisely because they refused to settle for the lower pleasures the world on offer.

Liberal Protestantism's appropriation of Puritan social vision — emphasis on education, civic responsibility, opposition to corruption, care for the poor — while abandoning the doctrinal core is precisely the trajectory H. Richard Niebuhr traced in The Kingdom of God in America (1937): the Puritan theology was progressively evacuated, leaving the ethical vocabulary without its theological ground. The social gospel that Walter Rauschenbusch preached was Puritan social concern detached from Puritan soteriology — the river without the source, which quickly runs shallow and then dry. The Puritan vision of the godly commonwealth was inseparable from the Puritan conviction that the regenerate conscience, renewed by the Spirit through the Word, was the only reliable engine of sustained social reform.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin purus (pure, unmixed) through English Puritan (one desiring to purify the church of Roman remnants); the movement drew on Calvin's Geneva, Bullinger's Zurich, and the Marian exiles' experience of Reformed churches on the Continent; its doctrinal architecture was Calvinist soteriology + Augustinian anthropology + regulative-principle ecclesiology + experimental spirituality.

expand to see more

English Puritan — first attested in the 1560s as a term of contempt for those who wished to purify the Church of England further from Roman Catholic residue; the label was accepted and resignified: the Puritans wore it as a badge of theological seriousness rather than allowing it to remain an insult.

Latin purus (pure, unmixed) — the root carries both cultic and moral sense: what is uncontaminated, unadulterated, unmixed with foreign element; the Puritan claim was that English Christianity was mixed with Roman alloy that the Reformation had not fully separated, and that pure religion required stripping the dross.

Latin experimentia (experience, trial, proof) — the Puritan tradition is often called “experimental Calvinism” because of its insistence that Reformed doctrine must be personally apprehended and practically applied; the “experimental” means tested-by-experience in the conscience and heart, not laboratory-experimental.

Greek katharismós (καθαρισμός) — purification, cleansing; the NT term for the ritual and moral cleansing that the law prescribed and Christ's blood accomplished; the Puritan project at the church level paralleled this: stripping the communion of everything that polluted pure apostolic worship.

English divinity — the Puritans' preferred term for what we call theology; “practical divinity” was their phrase for the application of theological truth to the soul; the distinction between speculative divinity (academic theology) and practical divinity (soul-work, conscience-work) drove the Puritan homiletical method.

Usage

"Reading the Puritans — Owen on mortification, Sibbes on Christ's bruised reed, Goodwin on the heart of Christ, Watson on the beatitudes, Flavel on the mystery of providence — is the single most efficient path to the combination of doctrinal rigor and pastoral warmth that the Reformed tradition at its best has always embodied."

"Puritan family worship (morning and evening prayer, Scripture reading, catechism, psalm-singing, father-led prayer) is not cultural nostalgia but the translation of the Deuteronomic household-instruction pattern (Deut 6:7) into a form suited to post-Reformation English life — a form recoverable in any culture willing to take seriously the father's priestly vocation in the home."

"The Puritan Sabbath — one day in seven withdrawn from labor, commerce, and entertainment and devoted to corporate worship, family instruction, and private devotion — is not legalism but the creational gift of rest applied with serious intentionality; its regular rhythm was the primary tool by which the Puritans prevented the secular week from colonizing the soul."
